about: A112/Atlas · DRAFTED DEFINITIONS for the Atlas's non-computing skills and tools, written by the agent in its own words (no source copied) for the OWNER'S REVIEW. Seeded at boot into atlas_nodes.definition_draft ONLY (definition_by = 'drafted') — never into `definition` — so nothing public shows them and the auto-publish bar does not count them until the owner accepts them in Admin → Atlas → Drafted definitions (D105 P11). A node that already has a definition or a waiting draft, or whose draft the owner rejected, is never touched; a slug with no node is skipped. Same rules as the chat import: one or two sentences, 20–400 characters, no links. Grouped by family; batch 1 (11-03): sales, finance & FP&A, accounting & audit, the three marketing families, product, workplace tools; batch 2a (11-03): people & HR, project & program management, operations & supply chain, consulting, business analysis. Left out on purpose (A114): store / hospitality terms (their roles are held as non-professional), boilerplate ('culture'), a misfiled node ('sales-growth'), the ambiguous 'oracle', and the second spelling of each duplicate pair (powerbi, ms-project, steering-committees, process-maps, brd, wbs, sar-filing, successfactors, toast-pos); batches 2b + 2c (11-03): design, legal practice, research & science, writing & communications. Also left out (A114): 'principle' (the common word matched as the Principle tool) and the second spelling of design-critique(s), press-release(s), copy-editing / copyediting, ediscovery / e-discovery, msas / master-services-agreements, ngs / next-generation-sequencing, wireframes / wireframing, user-research / ux-research; batch 2d (11-03): the six engineering families. Also left out (A114): 'safe' (523: the word matched as the SAFE software), 'mechanisms' (264, a common word), 'doors' (80: the word matched as IBM DOORS), the ambiguous 'soc', and the second spelling of v-v, dhf, fea, dfm, gn-c; batch 3 (11-03): the ROLES' definitions, every family (a role publishes on its postings alone; its definition shows above the board's data). The computing roles carry no stored family (roles are not drawn on the tree); they are grouped here under the family whose work they do, for reading only. Left out (A114): store / hospitality roles (branch-manager, hotel-general-manager, assistant-general-manager, practice-manager, site-manager) and the ambiguous portfolio-manager; batch 4c (11-03): the computing skills / tools that are NOT public on production (measured against /api/atlas/node/<slug>: 404) — no definition and no matched Wikipedia summary, often a short or ambiguous name (Go, Rust, R, C, Spark). One spelling kept per duplicate group (A114): spi / spi-protocol, i2c / i2c-protocol, jtag / jtag-debugging, trace32 / t32 / lauterbach / ltb / lauterbach-trace32-debugging / t32-debugging; batch 5 (11-03): the board roles' definitions (content/atlas/roles.json — roles the registry never named; seeded at boot BEFORE these drafts).

sales.salesforce: A customer relationship management platform where sales teams record accounts, contacts, opportunities and forecasts. Sellers use it to track every deal from first contact to close and managers use it to report on the pipeline.
sales.prospecting: Finding and researching potential customers who fit the company's target profile, then making first contact with them. It fills the top of the sales pipeline with new opportunities.
sales.consultative-selling: A sales approach in which the seller asks questions to understand a buyer's situation and problems before recommending a solution. The seller acts as an adviser rather than pushing a fixed product.
sales.sales-targets: The revenue, deal-count or activity goals a seller or team is expected to reach in a period. Pay and performance reviews in sales roles are usually tied to them.
sales.cold-calling: Telephoning prospective customers who have had no earlier contact with the company to introduce a product and book a conversation. It is a core activity in early-career sales development roles.
sales.outside-sales: Selling in person by visiting customers at their offices or sites, usually across an assigned territory. It contrasts with inside sales, which is done remotely.
sales.zoominfo: A business contact and company database that sales and marketing teams use to find prospects, phone numbers, emails and firmographic details. It is often connected to the CRM to enrich account records.
sales.product-demonstrations: Showing a prospective customer how a product works, live or recorded, focused on the problems that buyer cares about. A demo usually follows discovery and moves a deal toward evaluation.
sales.territory-management: Planning how a seller covers an assigned set of accounts or a region: which customers to prioritise, how often to contact them and how to grow revenue there.
sales.solution-selling: A sales method that starts from the customer's business problem and positions the product as the answer to it, rather than leading with features.
sales.closing-experience: A track record of taking sales opportunities through negotiation to a signed contract. Postings ask for it to show the seller has personally won deals, not only generated leads.
sales.closing-deals: Bringing a sales opportunity to a signed agreement by handling final objections, agreeing terms and securing the buyer's commitment.
sales.meddpicc: A sales qualification framework that checks a deal for metrics, economic buyer, decision criteria, decision process, paper process, identified pain, a champion and the competition. Teams use it to judge which deals are real and what is missing.
sales.cross-selling: Offering an existing customer additional products that complement what they already buy. It grows revenue from accounts the company already has.
sales.value-selling: Selling by quantifying the business value a customer will get, such as money saved or revenue gained, and anchoring the conversation and price on that value.
sales.new-business-development: Winning customers the company has never sold to before, as opposed to growing existing accounts. Roles focused on it are often called hunter roles.
sales.sales-methodology: A defined, repeatable way a sales team runs deals, such as a qualification framework or a selling approach that everyone on the team follows. It makes forecasting and coaching consistent.
sales.sales-calls: Phone or video conversations with prospects or customers to qualify, present, negotiate or follow up on a deal.
sales.quota-attainment: How much of an assigned sales quota a seller actually achieved, expressed as a percentage. Postings ask for a history of meeting or exceeding quota as evidence of performance.
sales.product-demos: Live or recorded walkthroughs of a product for a prospective customer, tailored to the problems that buyer described. A demo usually follows discovery in the sales process.
sales.inside-sales: Selling remotely by phone, email and video rather than in person. Inside sales teams often handle higher volumes of smaller or mid-sized deals.
sales.full-cycle-sales: Owning a deal from first prospecting through discovery, demo, negotiation and close, instead of handing it between specialised roles.
sales.clari: A revenue platform that pulls activity and deal data from the CRM, email and calendar to forecast sales and flag deals at risk.
sales.upselling: Persuading an existing customer to buy a higher tier, more seats or a larger version of what they already use.
sales.sales-forecasting: Predicting how much revenue the team will close in a period, based on the pipeline, each deal's stage and past win rates.
sales.president-s-club: An award many companies give their top-performing sellers each year, often with a trip. Postings mention it as a sign of a candidate's past sales results.
sales.discovery-calls: Early conversations with a prospect to learn their situation, problems, goals, budget and buying process before proposing anything.
sales.lead-qualification: Deciding whether a potential customer is worth pursuing by checking fit, need, budget, authority and timing. Qualified leads are passed on to account executives.
sales.mutual-action-plans: A shared document a seller and buyer agree on that lists the steps, owners and dates needed to reach a decision. It keeps complex deals on schedule.
sales.meddic: A sales qualification framework that checks a deal for metrics, economic buyer, decision criteria, decision process, identified pain and a champion. It helps sellers forecast accurately and focus on winnable deals.
sales.challenger-sale: A selling approach in which the seller teaches the customer something new about their business, tailors the message and takes control of the conversation, rather than simply building rapport.
sales.salesloft: A sales engagement platform that schedules and tracks sequences of emails, calls and tasks for sellers and records how prospects respond.
sales.linkedin-sales-navigator: LinkedIn's paid tool for sellers to search for prospects by company and role, save leads and follow account activity.
sales.seismic: A sales enablement platform that stores and recommends marketing content, decks and documents for sellers to share with buyers.
sales.cold-outreach: Contacting prospects who have had no earlier contact with the company, by email, phone or social messages, to start a sales conversation.
sales.spin-selling: A questioning method for sales conversations built on four question types: situation, problem, implication and need-payoff. It helps the buyer see the cost of their problem and the value of solving it.
sales.highspot: A sales enablement platform that organises content, playbooks and training for sellers and tracks how buyers engage with shared material.
sales.booked-meetings: Meetings a sales development representative schedules between a qualified prospect and an account executive. It is a common performance measure for those roles.
sales.pipedrive: A customer relationship management tool built around a visual sales pipeline, used mostly by smaller sales teams to track deals by stage.
sales.account-executive: A salesperson who owns deals with prospective customers, from discovery and demos through negotiation to close.
sales.account-manager: A person who looks after existing customers, keeping them satisfied and growing their business.
sales.sales-representative: A person who sells a company's products or services to customers.
sales.enterprise-account-executive: An account executive who sells to large organisations, handling long, complex deals.
sales.sales-manager: A manager who leads a sales team, setting targets and coaching sellers.
sales.sales-development-representative: An early-career salesperson who contacts and qualifies prospects and books meetings for account executives.
sales.senior-account-executive: An experienced account executive who handles larger or more complex deals.
sales.business-development-representative: An early-career salesperson who generates new leads and qualifies them for account executives.
sales.business-development-manager: A person who finds new business opportunities and partnerships and turns them into revenue.
sales.inside-sales-representative: A salesperson who sells remotely by phone, email and video.
sales.territory-sales-representative: A salesperson responsible for customers in an assigned geographic area.
sales.customer-success-manager: A person who makes sure customers get value from a product after they buy it, guiding adoption, renewals and growth.
sales.sales-engineer: A technical specialist who supports the sales team by explaining and demonstrating how a product meets a customer's technical needs.
sales.solutions-engineer: A technical specialist who works with sales to show prospective customers how the product solves their problems, through demos and proofs of concept.
sales.customer-engineer: A technical specialist who helps customers design, adopt and get value from a product, before or after the sale.
sales.account-director: A senior person who manages the relationship and revenue for an organisation's most important client accounts.
sales.partner-manager: A person who manages relationships with partner companies, such as resellers and technology partners, to grow joint business.
sales.business-development-executive: A salesperson who finds and wins new business for an organisation.
sales.sales-director: A senior sales leader who manages sales managers or a region and is responsible for its revenue.

fpa.forecasting: Estimating future results such as revenue, costs, demand or cash from past data, current trends and assumptions. Finance and operations teams update forecasts regularly to guide decisions.
fpa.treasury: The finance function that manages a company's cash, liquidity, bank relationships, borrowing, investments and currency or interest-rate risk.
fpa.portfolio-management: Choosing and managing a set of investments to meet return and risk goals, including deciding what to buy, hold or sell and rebalancing over time.
fpa.capital-markets: The markets where companies and governments raise money by issuing stocks and bonds, and where those securities are traded. Roles in this area structure, price, sell or trade such offerings.
fpa.financial-models: Spreadsheet models that project a business's revenue, costs, cash flow or value from a set of assumptions. They are used for planning, valuation and decisions such as investments or pricing.
fpa.p-l: The profit and loss statement, which reports a business's revenue, costs and resulting profit over a period. Roles that own a P&L are accountable for that unit's financial results.
fpa.valuation: Estimating what a company, asset or security is worth, using methods such as discounted cash flow, comparable companies and past transactions.
fpa.cfa: The Chartered Financial Analyst designation, a professional credential in investment analysis and portfolio management earned by passing three exams and meeting work-experience requirements.
fpa.management-reporting: Regular internal reports on financial and operating performance prepared for leaders, comparing results with budget and forecast and explaining the differences.
fpa.corporate-finance: The work of deciding how a company funds itself and invests its money, including capital structure, budgeting for investments, mergers and acquisitions and returning cash to shareholders.
fpa.variance-analysis: Comparing actual results with the budget or forecast and explaining why they differ, line by line.
fpa.bloomberg: The Bloomberg Terminal, a subscription system that delivers real-time market data, news, analytics and trading tools to finance professionals.
fpa.unit-economics: The revenue and costs tied to a single unit of a business, such as one customer or one order. It shows whether each unit is profitable and how that changes as the business grows.
fpa.scenario-analysis: Modelling how results would change under different sets of assumptions, such as a base, upside and downside case, to plan for uncertainty.
fpa.long-range-plan: A company's multi-year financial plan, usually three to five years, setting out expected growth, investments and profitability.
fpa.opex: Operating expenses: the ongoing costs of running a business, such as salaries, rent and software, as opposed to long-term capital investment.
fpa.annual-operating-plan: A company's budget and goals for the coming year, agreed by leadership, against which actual results are tracked.
fpa.credit-analysis: Judging how likely a borrower is to repay debt, by studying its financial statements, cash flows, collateral and industry risk.
fpa.working-capital: The money a business has tied up in its day-to-day operations, measured as current assets such as cash, receivables and inventory minus current liabilities such as payables.
fpa.hyperion: Oracle Hyperion, a family of enterprise performance-management software used for budgeting, forecasting, consolidation and financial reporting.
fpa.anaplan: A cloud planning platform used to build connected models for budgeting, forecasting, sales planning and workforce planning.
fpa.monthly-forecast: A forecast of revenue, costs or cash that finance updates each month with the latest results and assumptions.
fpa.budgeting-and-forecasting: Setting a financial plan for a period and then regularly re-estimating expected results as the period unfolds.
fpa.sensitivity-analysis: Testing how much a model's output changes when one input is changed at a time. It shows which assumptions matter most.
fpa.factset: A financial data and analytics platform that provides company financials, market data, estimates and screening tools to investment professionals.
fpa.equity-research: Analysing public companies and their shares to publish recommendations and price targets for investors, based on financial models and industry study.
fpa.capex: Capital expenditure: money spent on long-lived assets such as buildings, equipment or capitalised software, recorded on the balance sheet and depreciated over time.
fpa.board-reporting: Preparing the financial and operating materials presented to a company's board of directors, usually each quarter.
fpa.rolling-forecast: A forecast that always looks the same distance ahead, such as the next twelve months, adding a new period as each one closes.
fpa.dcf: Discounted cash flow, a valuation method that estimates what an asset is worth today by projecting its future cash flows and discounting them back by a required rate of return.
fpa.p-l-management: Being accountable for a business unit's revenue, costs and profit, including the decisions that move them.
fpa.capital-iq: S&P Capital IQ, a financial data platform with company financials, transaction records, ownership data and screening tools used in investment banking and research.
fpa.financial-modelling: Building spreadsheet models that project a business's revenue, costs, cash flow or value from a set of assumptions, to support planning, valuation and deals.
fpa.headcount-forecasting: Projecting how many people a company or team will employ over the planning period and what they will cost.
fpa.pitchbook: A data platform covering private companies, venture capital, private equity and mergers and acquisitions, used for deal sourcing and market research.
fpa.precedent-transactions: A valuation method that estimates a company's worth from the prices paid in past acquisitions of similar companies.
fpa.cash-flow-forecasting: Projecting the cash a business will receive and pay out over coming weeks or months, to make sure it can meet its obligations.
fpa.lbo: A leveraged buyout, the acquisition of a company funded largely with borrowed money, where the debt is repaid from the company's own cash flows.
fpa.cash-flow-analysis: Studying where a business's cash comes from and where it goes, across operating, investing and financing activities.
fpa.npv: Net present value: the value today of an investment's future cash flows, discounted at a required rate of return, minus its cost. A positive figure means the investment is expected to add value.
fpa.irr: Internal rate of return: the discount rate at which an investment's net present value is zero. It is used to compare the expected return of projects or deals.
fpa.adaptive-insights: Workday Adaptive Planning, a cloud tool for budgeting, forecasting and financial reporting.
fpa.essbase: Oracle Essbase, a multidimensional database used to store and analyse financial data for planning and reporting.
fpa.driver-based-models: Financial models in which results are calculated from a small number of operational drivers, such as headcount, price or volume, rather than entered line by line.
fpa.three-statement-model: A financial model that links the income statement, balance sheet and cash-flow statement so that a change to one assumption flows through all three.
fpa.refinitiv: A provider of financial market data, news and analytics, now part of the London Stock Exchange Group, used by traders and analysts.
fpa.comparable-company-analysis: A valuation method that estimates a company's worth from the trading multiples, such as price to earnings, of similar public companies.
fpa.planful: A cloud platform for financial planning, budgeting, consolidation and reporting.
fpa.budget-forecasting: Estimating future revenue and spending to set a budget, and re-estimating it as actual results come in.
fpa.driver-based-forecasting: Forecasting financial results from the operational drivers behind them, such as units sold, price or headcount.
fpa.budget-to-actual: A comparison of actual results with the budget for the same period, used to explain gaps and adjust plans.
fpa.capital-budgeting: Deciding which long-term investments, such as new equipment or projects, a company should fund, by comparing their expected returns and costs.
fpa.vena: A planning and budgeting platform built on Excel that adds a shared database, workflow and reporting for finance teams.
fpa.financial-analyst: An analyst who builds financial models, forecasts and reports to help an organisation plan and make decisions.
fpa.senior-financial-analyst: An experienced financial analyst who owns forecasts and analysis for a business area and guides junior analysts.
fpa.finance-manager: A manager who oversees financial planning, reporting and analysis for a business or team.
fpa.investment-analyst: An analyst who researches investments, builds valuation models and makes recommendations.
fpa.fp-a-analyst: An analyst in financial planning and analysis who builds budgets, forecasts and variance reports.
fpa.credit-analyst: An analyst who assesses whether borrowers can repay and recommends lending decisions.
fpa.portfolio-analyst: An analyst who monitors and analyses investment portfolios and their performance.
fpa.treasury-analyst: An analyst who manages cash, forecasts liquidity and supports banking and funding activities.
fpa.fp-a-manager: A manager who leads budgeting, forecasting and performance analysis for a business.
fpa.investment-banking-analyst: An early-career banker who builds models and materials for mergers, acquisitions and capital raising.
fpa.corporate-finance-analyst: An analyst who supports a company's funding, investment and capital decisions.
fpa.corporate-development-analyst: An analyst who supports a company's acquisitions, partnerships and investments.
fpa.equity-research-analyst: An analyst who studies public companies and publishes recommendations on their shares.
fpa.strategic-finance-manager: A finance manager who leads planning, modelling and analysis to support a company's strategic decisions.

accounting_audit.payroll: Calculating and paying employees' wages, withholding taxes and deductions, and filing the related tax reports on time.
accounting_audit.cpa: Certified Public Accountant, a licensed accounting credential in the United States earned by passing the CPA exam and meeting education and experience requirements.
accounting_audit.financial-reporting: Preparing a company's financial statements and related reports for leaders, investors, lenders or regulators, following accounting standards.
accounting_audit.netsuite: Oracle NetSuite, a cloud ERP system that runs a company's general ledger, billing, purchasing, inventory and financial reporting.
accounting_audit.gaap: Generally Accepted Accounting Principles, the standard rules companies follow when preparing financial statements. In the United States they are set by the Financial Accounting Standards Board.
accounting_audit.external-audit: An independent examination of a company's financial statements by an outside accounting firm, which gives an opinion on whether they are fairly presented.
accounting_audit.accruals: Accounting entries that record revenue when it is earned and expenses when they are incurred, even if cash has not yet changed hands.
accounting_audit.journal-entries: Records in the general ledger that post a transaction as equal debits and credits to the affected accounts.
accounting_audit.accounts-payable: The money a company owes its suppliers, and the team and process that check, approve and pay those invoices.
accounting_audit.accounts-receivable: The money customers owe a company for goods or services already delivered, and the process of invoicing and collecting it.
accounting_audit.sox-controls: Internal controls over financial reporting that public companies must design, document and test under the Sarbanes-Oxley Act.
accounting_audit.account-reconciliations: Checking that the balance of a general-ledger account matches supporting records, such as bank statements or subledgers, and explaining any difference.
accounting_audit.intercompany: Transactions between entities of the same group, such as a parent and its subsidiaries, which must be recorded on both sides and eliminated when the group's accounts are consolidated.
accounting_audit.revenue-accounting: Recording when and how much revenue a company recognises from its contracts, following standards such as ASC 606.
accounting_audit.close-process: The steps accounting completes at the end of each month, quarter or year to finalise the books, including reconciliations, accruals and review.
accounting_audit.us-gaap: The generally accepted accounting principles used in the United States, set by the Financial Accounting Standards Board.
accounting_audit.asc-606: The US accounting standard for revenue from contracts with customers. It sets out five steps for deciding when and how much revenue to recognise.
accounting_audit.tax-returns: The forms individuals and businesses file with tax authorities to report income and calculate the tax they owe.
accounting_audit.balance-sheet-reconciliations: Checking each balance-sheet account against supporting detail at period end and explaining or correcting any differences.
accounting_audit.indirect-tax: Taxes charged on transactions rather than on income, such as sales tax, VAT and GST, which businesses collect and pay to tax authorities.
accounting_audit.tax-provision: The calculation of a company's income-tax expense and the related current and deferred tax balances for its financial statements.
accounting_audit.vat: Value-added tax, a consumption tax charged at each stage of production and sale, which businesses collect and pass on to the tax authority.
accounting_audit.audit-support: Helping auditors by preparing schedules, documents and explanations they request during an audit.
accounting_audit.fixed-assets: Long-lived assets such as buildings, machinery and equipment, recorded on the balance sheet and depreciated over their useful lives.
accounting_audit.prepaids: Expenses paid in advance, such as insurance or software subscriptions, recorded as assets and expensed over the period they cover.
accounting_audit.gst: Goods and services tax, a value-added tax used in countries such as Canada, Australia and India.
accounting_audit.ifrs: International Financial Reporting Standards, the accounting standards issued by the IASB and used in most countries outside the United States.
accounting_audit.workiva: A cloud platform for preparing and filing financial reports, SEC filings and compliance documents, with linked data and review workflows.
accounting_audit.sales-and-use-tax: US state and local taxes on sales of goods and some services; use tax applies when sales tax was not charged at the time of purchase.
accounting_audit.pbc: Provided by client: the list of schedules and documents a company prepares and hands to its auditors.
accounting_audit.lease-accounting: Recording leases on the financial statements, including the right-of-use asset and lease liability required by ASC 842 and IFRS 16.
accounting_audit.blackline: A cloud platform that automates parts of the accounting close, including account reconciliations, journal entries and task tracking.
accounting_audit.avalara: Software that calculates, collects and files sales tax, VAT and other transaction taxes for businesses.
accounting_audit.oracle-financials: Oracle's financial software for the general ledger, payables, receivables and reporting, part of its ERP suites.
accounting_audit.audit-workpapers: The documents auditors prepare to record the procedures they performed, the evidence gathered and their conclusions.
accounting_audit.cost-accounting: Tracking and analysing what it costs to make a product or deliver a service, to support pricing, budgeting and cost control.
accounting_audit.quickbooks: Intuit's accounting software, widely used by small and mid-sized businesses for bookkeeping, invoicing and payroll.
accounting_audit.asc-842: The US accounting standard for leases. It requires most leases to appear on the balance sheet as a right-of-use asset and a lease liability.
accounting_audit.bank-reconciliations: Matching a company's cash records against its bank statements and explaining any differences.
accounting_audit.accounting-close: Finalising the accounting records at the end of a period so financial statements can be produced.
accounting_audit.sox-testing: Testing whether a company's internal controls over financial reporting are designed well and working, as the Sarbanes-Oxley Act requires.
accounting_audit.auditboard: A cloud platform for internal audit, SOX compliance and risk management work.
accounting_audit.sap-fico: The finance and controlling modules of SAP's ERP, covering the general ledger, payables, receivables, asset accounting and cost accounting.
accounting_audit.audit-fieldwork: The stage of an audit when the team gathers evidence, tests transactions and controls, and documents findings.
accounting_audit.sage-intacct: A cloud accounting and financial-management system used by mid-sized businesses.
accounting_audit.floqast: Close-management software that helps accounting teams organise month-end tasks and reconciliations.
accounting_audit.caseware: Software that auditors and accountants use to prepare working papers and financial statements.
accounting_audit.accountant: A professional who records, checks and reports an organisation's financial transactions and prepares its accounts.
accounting_audit.senior-accountant: An experienced accountant who owns parts of the close, reconciliations and reporting, and often reviews others' work.
accounting_audit.auditor: A professional who examines an organisation's financial records or controls to check they are accurate and comply with standards.
accounting_audit.accounting-manager: A manager who runs an accounting team and its month-end close, reporting and controls.
accounting_audit.controller: The senior accounting leader responsible for an organisation's books, financial reporting, controls and close.
accounting_audit.staff-accountant: An accountant who handles day-to-day entries, reconciliations and close tasks, usually early in their career.
accounting_audit.accounting-analyst: An analyst who supports accounting work such as reconciliations, journal entries and reporting.
accounting_audit.tax-accountant: An accountant who prepares tax returns and provisions and keeps an organisation or its clients compliant with tax rules.
accounting_audit.internal-auditor: An auditor employed by an organisation to test its own controls, processes and risks and report findings to management.
accounting_audit.audit-associate: An early-career auditor at an accounting firm who carries out audit procedures and documents evidence.
accounting_audit.tax-manager: A manager who leads tax compliance, planning and reporting for an organisation or its clients.

marketing_brand.go-to-market: The plan for bringing a product to market: which customers to target, how to position and price it, and which channels and teams will sell it.
marketing_brand.product-marketing: The marketing function that positions a product, defines its messaging and target buyers, supports launches and equips sales to sell it.
marketing_brand.brand-strategy: A long-term plan for how a company wants to be perceived, covering its positioning, personality, promise and the way it differs from competitors.
marketing_brand.brand-awareness: How familiar a target audience is with a brand, and the marketing work aimed at increasing that familiarity.
marketing_brand.brand-management: Looking after how a brand is presented and perceived over time, keeping its positioning, identity and messages consistent.
marketing_brand.market-segmentation: Dividing a market into groups of customers with shared needs or traits, so products and messages can be targeted at each.
marketing_brand.product-marketing-manager: A marketer who positions a product, defines its messaging and audience, leads launches and equips sales to sell it.
marketing_brand.brand-manager: A marketer responsible for a brand's positioning, image and growth across its campaigns and products.
marketing_brand.creative-strategist: A person who turns research about audiences and brands into the ideas and direction for creative campaigns.

marketing_content.social-media: Using platforms such as LinkedIn, Instagram, TikTok and X to publish content, engage an audience and promote a brand or product.
marketing_content.content-strategy: Planning what content an organisation creates, for which audience and purpose, and how it is produced, published and measured.
marketing_content.content-marketing: Attracting and keeping customers by publishing useful material, such as articles, guides, videos and newsletters, rather than direct advertising.
marketing_content.email-marketing: Sending marketing messages to a list of subscribers or customers by email, from newsletters to automated sequences, and measuring opens, clicks and conversions.
marketing_content.mailchimp: An email marketing platform for building subscriber lists, designing campaigns, automating sequences and reporting on results.
marketing_content.klaviyo: An email and SMS marketing platform, popular with e-commerce brands, for automated flows and segmented campaigns.
marketing_content.influencer-marketing: Working with creators who have engaged audiences on social media to promote a brand or product.
marketing_content.lifecycle-campaigns: Marketing messages timed to a customer's stage, from onboarding to renewal or win-back, to keep them engaged and buying.
marketing_content.sprout-social: A social media management platform for scheduling posts, managing messages, listening and reporting across networks.
marketing_content.hootsuite: A social media management tool for scheduling posts, monitoring mentions and reporting across several networks.
marketing_content.email-flows: Automated sequences of emails triggered by a customer's behaviour, such as signing up, abandoning a cart or making a purchase.
marketing_content.content-marketing-manager: A marketer who plans and produces content, such as articles, guides and video, to attract and keep customers.
marketing_content.lifecycle-marketing-manager: A marketer who runs the messages customers receive at each stage of their relationship, such as onboarding, retention and win-back.

marketing_digital.pipeline-generation: Creating new qualified sales opportunities through marketing and outreach, measured by the value of pipeline sourced.
marketing_digital.demand-generation: Marketing aimed at creating interest in a product and turning it into qualified leads and sales pipeline, across campaigns, content and channels.
marketing_digital.paid-media: Advertising a company pays for, such as search ads, social ads, display and video, as opposed to earned or owned media.

eng_process.supply-chain-engineer: An engineer who designs and improves supply chain networks, flows and operations.
eng_process.lean-engineer: An engineer who applies lean methods to remove waste from processes.

backend.software-engineer: An engineer who designs, writes, tests and maintains software, working with others to turn requirements into reliable, well-structured code.
backend.full-stack-engineer: A software engineer who builds both the user-facing parts of an application and the servers, APIs and databases behind them.
backend.software-developer: A person who writes, tests and maintains software applications, turning requirements into working code.
backend.backend-engineer: A software engineer who builds the server side of applications: APIs, business logic, databases and the services that support them.
backend.staff-engineer: A senior individual-contributor engineer who leads technical direction across several teams, designing large systems and raising the quality of others' work.
backend.frontend-engineer: A software engineer who builds the parts of web applications that users see and interact with, using HTML, CSS and JavaScript frameworks.
backend.android-engineer: A software engineer who builds apps for Android devices, usually in Kotlin or Java.
backend.mobile-engineer: A software engineer who builds applications for phones and tablets on iOS, Android or both.
backend.payments-engineer: A software engineer who builds the systems that move money, such as checkout, billing, payment processing and reconciliation.
backend.test-automation-engineer: An engineer who writes code and frameworks that test software automatically, so problems are caught before release.
backend.ui-engineer: A software engineer focused on building user interfaces, turning designs into accessible, responsive and well-behaved screens.
backend.rest-apis: Web interfaces that let programs exchange data over HTTP using standard methods such as GET and POST on named resources. Most web and mobile backends expose their features this way.
backend.object-oriented: A way of structuring programs around objects that bundle data with the code that acts on it, using ideas such as classes, encapsulation and inheritance.
backend.go: Go, a compiled programming language from Google known for simple syntax, fast builds and built-in concurrency. It is widely used for backend services, infrastructure tools and cloud software.
backend.advanced-algorithms: Algorithms beyond the basics, such as graph algorithms, dynamic programming and approximation methods, used to solve hard problems efficiently.
backend.payments-platforms: Systems that accept, process and settle payments, handling cards, bank transfers, fraud checks and reconciliation.
backend.android-development: Building apps for Android devices, usually in Kotlin or Java with Android's SDK and tools.
backend.multi-tier-systems: Applications split into separate layers, such as presentation, business logic and data, that run and scale independently.
backend.ui-implementation: Turning interface designs into working, accessible and responsive screens in code.
backend.web-applications: Applications that run in a web browser and talk to servers over the internet, from simple sites to complex online tools.
backend.swift: Apple's programming language for building apps on iOS, macOS and its other platforms.
backend.selenium: An open-source framework for automating web browsers, used mainly to test web applications.
backend.playwright: An open-source framework from Microsoft for automating browsers to test web applications across Chromium, Firefox and WebKit.
backend.engineering-manager: A manager who leads a team of software engineers, hiring and developing them and making sure the team delivers reliable work on time.
backend.forward-deployed-engineer: A software engineer who works directly with customers, building and adapting the product inside their environment to solve their problems.
backend.ios-engineer: A software engineer who builds apps for iPhone and iPad, usually in Swift.
backend.salesforce-developer: A developer who customises and extends Salesforce with code, configuration and integrations.

systems.security-engineer: An engineer who protects an organisation's systems and data by designing defences, finding vulnerabilities and responding to threats.
systems.performance-engineer: An engineer who measures how fast and efficiently software or systems run, finds bottlenecks and makes them faster.
systems.systems-software-engineer: A software engineer who works close to the hardware and operating system, building drivers, runtimes, kernels or low-level libraries.
systems.firmware-engineer: An engineer who writes the low-level software that runs directly on hardware devices such as microcontrollers.
systems.platform-software-engineer: A software engineer who builds the low-level software platform a product runs on, such as boot code, drivers and system services.
systems.operating-systems-engineer: An engineer who builds and improves operating system components, such as the kernel, scheduler, memory management and drivers.
systems.graphics-engineer: A software engineer who builds rendering systems and graphics code for games, design tools or devices, often working with the GPU.
systems.embedded-software-engineer: A software engineer who writes code for devices with limited resources, such as microcontrollers in consumer, automotive or industrial products.
systems.systems-performance-engineer: An engineer who analyses and tunes the performance of whole systems, from hardware and operating system to application.
systems.embedded-systems-engineer: An engineer who designs devices that combine hardware and software for a dedicated function, and writes the software that runs on them.
systems.device-driver-engineer: An engineer who writes the software that lets an operating system communicate with a hardware device.
systems.bsp-engineer: An engineer who builds the board support package, the low-level code that lets an operating system run on a specific circuit board.
systems.board-support-package-engineer: An engineer who builds the low-level code, such as boot loaders and drivers, that lets an operating system run on a specific board.
systems.rtos-engineer: An engineer who builds or works with real-time operating systems, which must respond to events within strict time limits.
systems.hardware-debug-engineer: An engineer who finds and fixes problems where hardware and low-level software meet, using debuggers, probes and analysers.
systems.firmware-debug-engineer: An engineer who investigates and fixes faults in firmware running on devices, often with hardware debugging tools.
systems.soc-bring-up-engineer: An engineer who gets a new system-on-chip working for the first time, running early software and finding hardware and firmware problems.
systems.chip-bring-up-engineer: An engineer who powers up and tests newly manufactured chips, getting their first software running and finding defects.
systems.post-silicon-validation-engineer: An engineer who tests manufactured chips against their specifications to find design bugs before the product ships.
systems.kernel-engineer: An engineer who works on an operating system kernel, the core code that manages processes, memory and hardware.
systems.compiler-engineer: An engineer who builds compilers, the programs that translate source code into efficient machine code.
systems.software-tools-engineer: An engineer who builds the internal tools, such as build systems, debuggers and test frameworks, that other engineers use.
systems.computer-vision-engineer: An engineer who builds systems that interpret images and video, using image processing and machine learning.
systems.audio-video-engineer: An engineer who builds software for capturing, processing, encoding or playing audio and video.
systems.wireless-software-engineer: An engineer who writes software for wireless communication, such as Wi-Fi, Bluetooth or cellular protocols.
systems.performance-optimisation: Making software or systems faster or more efficient by measuring where time and resources go and removing bottlenecks.
systems.concurrency: Structuring a program so several tasks make progress at once, and handling the coordination and shared data that this requires.
systems.multithreading: Running several threads of execution within one program so work can proceed in parallel or overlap waiting.
systems.firmware-development: Writing the low-level software that runs directly on a device's hardware, such as a microcontroller.
systems.gdb: The GNU Debugger, a command-line tool for stepping through programs, inspecting memory and finding bugs.
systems.kernel-drivers: Software modules inside an operating system kernel that control hardware devices.
systems.board-bring-up: Getting a new circuit board working for the first time: powering it, loading early software and finding hardware and firmware faults.
systems.bsp: A board support package: the boot code, drivers and configuration that let an operating system run on a particular board.
systems.registers-and-memory: The low-level view of hardware as registers and memory addresses that software reads and writes to control a device.
systems.hardware-software-co-debug: Finding faults that span hardware and software together, using debuggers, probes and analysers on the running system.
systems.peripherals: Hardware blocks attached to a processor, such as timers, serial interfaces and controllers, and the software that drives them.
systems.low-level-diagnostics: Tests and tools that check hardware and low-level software directly to locate faults.
systems.pcie-debugging: Finding and fixing problems on PCI Express links between devices, such as link training, enumeration or data errors.
systems.protocol-debugging: Finding faults in how devices communicate over a protocol, by capturing and analysing the traffic between them.
systems.silicon-validation: Testing manufactured chips against their specifications to find design bugs before a product ships.
systems.real-time-systems: Systems that must respond to events within strict time limits, such as control systems in vehicles or machines.
systems.soc-bring-up: Getting a new system-on-chip working for the first time, running its first software and finding hardware and firmware problems.
systems.trace32: Lauterbach's TRACE32 debugger and trace tools for embedded processors, used to debug code running on target hardware.
systems.zephyr: The Zephyr Project, an open-source real-time operating system for small embedded and connected devices.
systems.jtag: A standard hardware interface for testing circuit boards and debugging processors on them.
systems.openocd: An open-source tool that connects a debugger such as GDB to embedded processors through JTAG or similar interfaces.
systems.c: C, a compiled programming language that gives direct control over memory, used for operating systems, embedded software and performance-critical code.
systems.lldb: The debugger from the LLVM project, used to step through programs and inspect their state.
systems.logic-analyzer: An instrument that captures and displays many digital signals over time, used to debug circuits and protocols.
systems.oscilloscope: An instrument that shows how voltage signals change over time, used to test and debug electronic circuits.
systems.spi: Serial Peripheral Interface, a simple, fast serial bus for connecting a processor to chips such as sensors and memory.
systems.uart: A universal asynchronous receiver-transmitter, the hardware for simple serial communication between devices.
systems.can: Controller Area Network, a robust serial bus that lets controllers in vehicles and machines communicate.
systems.i2c: Inter-Integrated Circuit, a two-wire serial bus for connecting a processor to low-speed chips such as sensors.
systems.kernel-development: Writing and changing the core of an operating system, such as its scheduler, memory management and drivers.
systems.software-tools: The tools developers use to build, test and debug software, such as compilers, build systems and debuggers, and the work of building them.
systems.compiler-engineering: Building compilers and related tools that translate and optimise source code into machine code.
systems.operating-systems: The software that manages a computer's hardware and runs programs, and the study of how it schedules work, manages memory and handles devices.
systems.performance-profiling: Measuring where a program spends its time and resources, to find what to optimise.
systems.debug-tooling: Tools that help engineers find faults, such as debuggers, tracers and logging, and the work of building them.
systems.latency-optimisation: Reducing the time a system takes to respond to a request or event.
systems.runtime-systems: The software that supports a program while it runs, such as memory management, garbage collection and thread scheduling.
systems.systems-performance: How fast and efficiently a whole system runs across hardware, operating system and application, and the work of measuring and improving it.
systems.perf: The Linux perf tool, which uses hardware and software counters to profile where programs spend their time.
systems.rust: Rust, a compiled programming language that prevents many memory errors at compile time without a garbage collector, used for systems and performance-critical software.
systems.gcc: The GNU Compiler Collection, the open-source compilers for C, C++ and other languages.
systems.compilers-and-tools: Compilers together with the linkers, debuggers and build tools that turn source code into running programs.
systems.graphics-and-imaging: Software that draws, renders or processes images, from 2D graphics to 3D rendering and image pipelines.
systems.audio-video-systems: Systems that capture, encode, process and play audio and video.
systems.windows-development: Building software for Microsoft Windows, from desktop applications to drivers and system components.
systems.wireless-applications: Software and systems that communicate over wireless links such as Wi-Fi, Bluetooth or cellular.

infra.platform-engineer: An engineer who builds the shared infrastructure and tools that other engineering teams use to build, deploy and run their software.
infra.site-reliability-engineer: An engineer who keeps production systems reliable and fast, using software to automate operations, monitor services and respond to incidents.
infra.infrastructure-engineer: An engineer who designs and runs the servers, networks, cloud resources and automation that applications depend on.
infra.distributed-systems-engineer: An engineer who builds software that runs across many machines, dealing with coordination, consistency and failures between them.
infra.docker: A platform for packaging an application and everything it needs into a container that runs the same way on any machine.
infra.prometheus: An open-source monitoring system that collects metrics from services as time series and raises alerts on them.
infra.security-and-cryptography: Protecting systems and data from attack, including the use of encryption, hashing, signatures and key management.
infra.windows: Microsoft's operating system for personal computers and servers, and the work of developing for or administering it.
infra.solutions-architect: A technical expert who designs how a product or platform should be used to meet a customer's requirements, often working alongside sales.
infra.devops-engineer: An engineer who automates how software is built, tested, deployed and operated, bridging development and operations.
infra.network-engineer: An engineer who designs, builds and maintains computer networks.
infra.support-engineer: An engineer who investigates and resolves customers' technical problems with a product.

data.data-scientist: A person who uses statistics, programming and machine learning to analyse data, build models and answer business questions.
data.data-engineer: An engineer who builds the pipelines and storage that collect, clean and move data so others can analyse and use it.
data.research-scientist: A scientist who carries out original research, designing experiments and publishing or applying the results to advance a field or product.
data.data-analyst: A person who collects, cleans and analyses data and turns it into reports and insights that help others make decisions.
data.analytics-engineer: A person who turns raw data into clean, tested and documented data models that analysts and dashboards rely on.
data.quantitative-analyst: A person who uses mathematics, statistics and programming to model financial markets, price securities or manage risk.
data.business-intelligence-analyst: A person who builds dashboards and reports from company data and explains trends to help leaders make decisions.
data.database-internals: How databases work inside: storage engines, indexes, query planning, transactions and recovery.
data.spark: Apache Spark, an open-source engine for processing large datasets in parallel across a cluster, used for batch jobs, streaming and machine learning.
data.kafka: Apache Kafka, an open-source platform for streaming events, which stores ordered logs of messages that many systems can publish to and read from.
data.airflow: Apache Airflow, an open-source tool for scheduling and monitoring data pipelines written as Python workflows.
data.statistical-modelling: Building mathematical models of data that describe relationships and uncertainty, such as regression models, to explain or predict outcomes.
data.data-warehousing: Collecting data from many sources into one central store organised for analysis and reporting.
data.etl: Extract, transform, load: the process of pulling data from source systems, cleaning and reshaping it, and loading it into a store for analysis.
data.dbt: An open-source tool that lets analysts and engineers transform data in a warehouse using version-controlled SQL with tests and documentation.
data.r: R, a programming language and environment for statistics, data analysis and graphics.
data.hypothesis-testing: Statistical methods for deciding whether data provide enough evidence to reject an assumption, such as that two groups do not differ.
data.data-visualisation: Presenting data as charts, maps and graphics so patterns and comparisons are easy to see.
data.looker: Google's business intelligence platform for exploring data and building dashboards on a modelled layer over the warehouse.
data.tableau: Salesforce's data visualisation software for building interactive charts and dashboards.
data.pandas: A Python library for loading, cleaning, reshaping and analysing tabular data.
data.databricks: A cloud data platform built around Apache Spark for data engineering, analytics and machine learning on a shared lakehouse.
data.jupyter: Jupyter notebooks, documents that combine live code, results, charts and text, widely used for data analysis.
data.product-analyst: An analyst who studies how people use a product, through data and experiments, to guide product decisions.

ml.ml-engineer: An engineer who builds, trains and deploys machine learning models and the systems that serve them in production.
ml.model-deployment: Putting a trained machine learning model into production so applications can use its predictions, and keeping it running and monitored.
ml.nlp: Natural language processing: methods that let computers analyse, understand and generate human language.
ml.mlflow: An open-source platform for tracking machine learning experiments, packaging models and managing their deployment.
ml.ai-engineer: An engineer who builds products and features on top of AI models, such as language models, including their prompts, data, evaluation and deployment.
ml.research-engineer: An engineer who builds the code, experiments and infrastructure that research teams need, turning research ideas into working systems.
